title: An island (24–28)
hook: by effort and restraint the wise make an island no flood can overwhelm

segments.voice: Yesterday, appamada, heedfulness, and your line: heedful is alive. Which task did you do with full attention? Day one hundred sixty-three.

In the Ganges plain, the monsoon floods can spread for miles. Fields vanish. Roads vanish. From above, the land is a sheet of brown water. But here and there you see them: small patches of raised ground where a village has built up the earth, year after year, basket by basket, so that when the water rises, there's still somewhere dry to stand. Nobody builds that in one season. And nobody builds it during the flood. Today, verses twenty-four to twenty-eight: an island.
screen: `THE MONSOON FLOOD.` → `RAISED GROUND, BASKET BY BASKET.` → `NOT BUILT DURING THE FLOOD.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-five, in Müller's English: “By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.” Four tools: rousing yourself, heedfulness, restraint and self-control. And one result: an island. In the Buddha's teaching, the flood is a standing image for the currents that sweep people along: craving, views, ignorance, the endless round. You can't stop the river. You can raise the ground you stand on. The word for island is dipa. And here's a lovely puzzle: in Pali, dipa can mean island, and it can also mean lamp. When the Buddha, near the end of his life, told his followers to be a dipa for themselves, translators split. Rhys Davids gave lamps. Many modern translators give islands. The tradition has lived with both. The commentary tells verse twenty-five about a monk called Little Panthaka. For four months he couldn't memorize a single verse; it slipped away as soon as he learned the next line. His brother, also a monk, told him to give up and go home. The Buddha found him crying outside the monastery, handed him a clean white cloth, and told him to rub it while repeating a simple phrase about removing dirt. As he rubbed, the cloth grew grimy in his hand, and he saw, in that small change, how everything changes. The story says he awakened right there. The verses around it add that fools give themselves to carelessness, while the wise guard heedfulness like their best treasure. No one built Panthaka's island with scholarship. He built it with one small practice, repeated.
screen: `FOUR TOOLS, ONE ISLAND.` · `THE FLOOD: WHAT SWEEPS US ALONG.` · `DIPA — ISLAND, OR LAMP.` · `LITTLE PANTHAKA AND THE WHITE CLOTH.` · then, large: `MAKE AN ISLAND.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of the flood in your own life: the busiest week, the hard news, the tired evening when everything slides. Now ask: what small thing, done every day, would give me somewhere dry to stand? Maybe it's this sit. Maybe three breaths before opening email. Maybe a walk after dinner. Choose one small habit, small enough that you could keep it even on a bad day. Picture yourself doing it tomorrow, then the next day. One basket of earth at a time. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
An island. The raised ground the wise build, by effort and restraint, so that no flood can overwhelm them.
Your line: make an island. Today, begin the small daily habit you chose, and do it once, even if it takes one minute. Day one hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the island verse to describe steady daily practice as a refuge, and the story of Culapanthaka and the white cloth is a favorite example of awakening through one simple, repeated practice.

fork.reveal: the Buddha found him, gave him a clean cloth and a phrase about removing dirt. watching the cloth grow grimy, he saw how everything changes.

original.note: Pali: island, and also lamp: the word behind 'make an island.'

trapdoor: what you thought: the island means cutting yourself off from other people.
what it means: raised ground, built by steady effort, where you can stand when the flood comes.
what a scholar hears: Pali dipa covers Sanskrit dvipa (island) and dipa (lamp); translators of 'attadipa' in DN 16 have split between 'lamp' and 'island.'

sources.quoted: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.

notes: Culapanthaka story simplified (the phrase given is rajoharanam, 'removing dirt'); confirm.
Claim that Rhys Davids rendered DN 16's attadipa as 'lamps' ('be ye lamps unto yourselves'): confirm.
The flood (ogha) as the currents of sensuality, becoming, views and ignorance is a standard sutta image; kept general here.
